newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Head of African group coy on chance of U.N. post.
newsitem.headline: Head of African group coy on chance of U.N. post.

text.p: The head of the Organisation for African Unity denied he was a candidate to be the next U.N. secretary-general, but played coy on whether he might accept a nomination.

Salim Salim, mentioned as a possible successor to current U.N. head Boutros Boutros-Ghali, made his comments after talks on Thursday at OAU headquarters here with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
One of Christopher's top objectives on his five-nation Africa tour this week is to talk with African leaders about the U.S. insistence that Boutros-Ghali leave office when his term ends in December.
Washington says Boutros-Ghali is not reform-minded enough to lead the world body into the 21st century.

Enroute to Africa, Christopher warned African leaders that failure to start proposing alternatives to Boutros-Ghali might mean Africa will lose the opportunity to have an African in the secretary-general's job for another term.

There seems an increasing possibility the United States may have to make good on its threat to veto the reappointment of Boutros-Ghali, an Egyptian backed by the OAU, before Africa will come forward with an alternative.
"Am I a candidate? I'm not a candidate," Salim, from Tanzania, told a news conference, repeating his oft-stated position. He says he is looking forward to a new term at the OAU.
But pressed by a reporter to say whether he would not accept the U.N. job under any circumstances, Salim appeared to leave his options open, replying: "Even if I say that, you won't believe me.
"I've been there before. In 1981 I was the only African candidate proposed by the African leaders, unanimously supported by so many countries, and I didn't make it.
"Having gone through that experience I think I'm a bit wiser in terms of saying whether I'm going to be a candidate or not," he added.

He said the question of the U.N. secretary-generalship did not come up in his meeting with Christopher. But U.S. officials said Christopher asked Salim about a host of Africa-related regional problems, including Somalia, Sudan, Zaire and Angola.
While this might be expected of a U.S. secretary of state on his first visit to sub-Saharan Africa, it also could serve a double-purpose as a job interview.
Christopher, at a separate news conference, said no new names were proposed for secretary-general in the Salim meeting.
"I have high regard for Secretary-General Salim, for his leadership in Africa, and I think he's widely recognised for having done a good job at the OAU."
But the United States does not have a favourite candidate "and I don't have any comment on his possible candidacy except to say he's a well-recognised leader in Africa," he said.
Salim, asked if Africa would offer another candidate besides Boutros-Ghali, said: "I think we'll answer the question when the time comes."
If it becomes evident U.S. opposition to Boutros-Ghali is "irreversible", Africa would have "good, eminent and effective candidates" to propose, he said.

Kofi Annan of Ghana, U.N. undersecretary general for peacekeeping, is also mentioned as a possible candidate but some say he is too allied to Washington. Hamid Algabid of Niger, head of the Islamic Conference, has announced his candidacy.
